# Registration Scope Plan

A clause planner that adds a native registration-pattern matcher to generated connection handlers. Its purpose is to make an owner-approved registration constraint available for matching actor-supplied values, without treating those values as grant rules or executable code.

## Registration pattern

`plan` calls `planRegistrationScopes`, which reads `parameters/registrationPattern` from the candidate clause’s definition view. The pattern must be an object; otherwise planning fails with `MANDATE_REGISTRATION_PATTERN_REQUIRED`. No default or more specific pattern schema is established here.

After calling inherited `planConnections`, it adds `qualifiesRegistration(candidate)` to the first Compute step of every contribution whose `kind` is `handler`, including timer arm and cancel handlers. This function applies native `$is` matching to `candidate` using the literal pattern. Planning does not evaluate the pattern as executable instructions.

The generated wrapper does not itself call `qualifiesRegistration`. Registration acceptance therefore depends on the action that uses the helper; installing it establishes neither an accepted registration nor proof of owner approval. The planner returns the generated `contracts`, `states` and `reads`; returning a plan is not confirmation of installation or execution.

## Inherited configuration

- `type/defaultBindings` supplies bindings overridden by the clause’s `bindings`. Property bindings must be declared in `type/bindingTypes`; bindings naming actions or `type/childActions` are handled separately. Required property bindings must have the declared kind. A `pointer` binding must be text beginning with `/`, other than `/` itself. `type/optionalBindings` permits omission, but supplied values are still checked.
- Actions come from `type/actions`, or from `parameters/actions` when `type/configurableActions` is `true`. If actions are absent, an object-valued `type/initialState` permits an empty action set. Structural initial state requires named pointer bindings and object initial values.
- Each action binding is a dictionary of named connections. An action’s `automatic` declaration adds a reserved `_automatic` connection; an explicit connection cannot replace it. Clause, action and connection names must be nonempty and contain no `.`, `/` or `~`. Unsupported connection fields and unknown names in `parameters/conditions` are rejected.
- `type/embeds` and `type/embedsCollections` identify declared pointer bindings for embedded processing. Connections using `embedded` or `collection` also request embedding unless `embed` is explicitly `false`.
- Normally, generated handlers receive clause parameters excluding `actions` and `conditions`. With `type/readParametersFromDocument=true`, their `parameters` constant is empty. `type/snapshotBindings` captures available bound document values during planning; an available snapshot binding must identify an existing value. An optional `type/actionDefinition` supplies the generated Compute definition identity.

Supported `on` declarations are `event`, `embedded`, `collection`, `change`, `channel`, `initialized`, `activated`, `workflow` and `timer`. Path-based sources require non-root JSON pointers. `channel` refers to an existing named channel. A `workflow` connection produces an operation using `party` when supplied, otherwise `channel`, and can carry `request` and `event` declarations. A callable operation or channel name alone establishes no caller permission.

`validateConfiguration` returns an allowed result, but planning still performs the checks above. `validateTransition` allows only an unchanged clause at the existing key; a changed candidate returns `CONNECTIONS_REQUIRE_NEW_CLAUSE_KEY`.

## Generated action execution

`once` defaults to `false`. When enabled, an already true `fired` flag makes subsequent invocations return immediately. Collection handlers also ignore events outside descendants of their configured `path`.

The action’s `trigger` is the workflow request, the inner event for embedded or collection sources, the captured arming trigger for timers, or the incoming event for other sources. Action `defaults` are merged with connection `params`, with connection values taking precedence; both default to empty objects. Connection `when` defaults to `true`; a false result skips the action.

The wrapper then checks action `args`, `require/when` and `parameters/conditions/<actionName>`. Failures reject with `ACTION_ARGUMENT_INVALID`, the configured requirement message or `ACTION_REQUIREMENT_FAILED`, and `ACTION_CONDITION_FAILED`, respectively. Missing requirement and condition expressions default to `true`.

If `preflight` exists, it must set `actionResult.outcome` to `acceptedNew`, `duplicate`, `rejected` or `skipped`. Only `acceptedNew` proceeds to connection `before`, action `do`, and subsequent processing. With `resultContract="outcome-v1"`, the action body must also produce one of those outcomes; only `acceptedNew` proceeds to `after` and the one-time completion flag. The default `resultContract` is `legacy`, which does not impose that post-action outcome check. Returning early for another outcome does not itself undo effects already produced by the action.

## Timers and connection state

A timer requires exactly one of `timestamp` and `afterEvent`:

- `timestamp` is an integer Unix-microsecond deadline from `0` through `9007199254740991`. It arms from initialization and cannot be combined with `delayMs` or an explicit `policy`.
- `afterEvent` uses a timestamped source and a positive integer `delayMs`, at most `9007199254740` milliseconds. The deadline is derived from that source’s logical timestamp and must remain within the same timestamp range. Initialization cannot supply this relative timer’s source. Timer source selectors support `event`, `embedded`, `collection`, `change`, `channel` and, where applicable, `initialized`.

Relative timer `policy` defaults to `first`, which ignores later arming inputs once `armed` is true. `latest` emits replacement requests using the same key, `connection`. With `once=true`, a completed one-time action also prevents later arming. Optional `cancelOn` must name a source and emits a cancellation request for that key.

Requests require the native Time runtime. Only committed effects establish or cancel registrations; a scheduling request is not a firing or confirmation that the action ran. New deadlines must follow the invocation’s logical position, with the Time protocol’s exception for standalone initialization without a prior external position. Firing also requires a still-pending registration and ordered-history evidence. Cancellation of an absent pending key is harmless and cannot undo an earlier firing.

The plan proposes `/connectionState_{clauseKey}` with one entry per `actionName.connectionName`, initially containing `armed=false` and `fired=false`. These defaults apply only when initialization is installed. `armed` becomes true when a timer arming handler records a scheduling request; it is not a current pending-timer status. `fired` becomes true only when a `once=true` action reaches the end of its wrapper after `after`. It is not a general timer-firing or registration-success flag. Neither flag is cleared by the supplied firing or cancellation code, so cancelling a timer does not enable rearming under `first`. Missing state means unknown.
